title: Rook behind the passed pawn
summary: Tarrasch's rule: the rook belongs behind the passed pawn, yours and your opponent's.
part.own.title: Behind your own pawn
part.own.summary: The same pieces with the rooks swapped: behind wins, in front draws.
part.get.title: Getting behind
part.get.summary: Bringing the rook behind the pawn, and getting there before the enemy rook.
part.theirs.title: Behind the enemy pawn
part.theirs.summary: In defence the rook also goes behind the pawn; in front of it, the rook is tied down.
part.rules.title: Recap
part.rules.summary: Tarrasch's rule, the exception that cost Kramnik a game, and practice against the machine.
step.t_behind: You play White and have a passed pawn on the a-file. Look at where each rook stands. Can Black hold this pawn? And what is your plan to win?
step.t_behind.hint1: Compare the two rooks. How many squares does each have on the a-file, and how many will it have when the pawn advances?
step.t_behind.hint2: The black rook cannot leave the front of the pawn. So your king is the one who helps the pawn, and Black has only the king to defend both the pawn and the kingside.
step.behind: Your rook is behind the pawn, the black rook is in front of it. Look at the difference. With every step the pawn takes, your rook gains one more square on the file and keeps protecting the pawn. The black rook does the opposite: it loses squares. With the pawn on a7 it has only a8, and if it leaves, the pawn queens. One rook has become a guard; the other is free. This is the rule Siegbert Tarrasch wrote down more than a hundred years ago: the rook belongs behind the passed pawn.
step.front: Now the same pieces, with the rooks swapped. Your rook stands in front of the pawn and has nowhere to go: it blocks its own pawn. The black rook, behind it, attacks the pawn and checks your king from a distance if it tries to come closer. Black keeps the king on g7 or h7 and waits. And that is a draw. Same pieces, same side to move: only the rooks' placement changed the result.
step.d_walk: Watch how White wins the good position. The idea is simple: the black rook is tied down, so your king walks to the pawn.
step.d_walk.m1: a7! The pawn advances and the black rook is pinned to a8. If it leaves the file, the pawn queens with your rook's protection.
step.d_walk.m2: The black king heads for the centre.
step.d_walk.m3: Your king sets off towards the pawn. No hurry: Black has nothing to do.
step.d_walk.m4: Black decides to guard the g6 pawn.
step.d_walk.m6: The black king can only wait.
step.d_walk.m8: Now the black king tries to come back to the queenside, but it is late.
step.d_walk.m9: The white king arrives first and controls b7.
step.d_walk.m10: The black king cannot step onto c7: the white king guards that square.
step.d_walk.m11: Kb7 attacks the rook. It has to leave a8, and the pawn promotes with your rook's support. Notice that the white rook never had to move: behind the pawn, it works while standing still.
step.twoTargets: Now you play. Advance the pawn and bring the king to the centre. If the black king runs to the queenside, go and take the g6 pawn.
step.twoTargets.hint: a7, then Kf3, Ke4, Kf4 and Kg5. The rook stays on the a-file.
step.twoTargets.done: The black king went to stop the a-pawn and abandoned the g-pawn. Two targets for one king. The black rook helps with neither, because it is stuck in front of the pawn.
step.t_side: The black rook attacks your pawn from the side. Only one move keeps the win. Which one?
step.t_side.hint1: Look for the square from which the rook protects the pawn and still gains room when it advances.
step.side: Ra1. The rook goes behind the pawn: it protects the pawn and gains a square with every advance. To stop the pawn, the black rook will have to stand in front of it, tied down as in the previous position. Any other move loses the pawn and the win.
step.ra1: Bring the rook behind the pawn.
step.ra1.hint: Along the first rank, to the a-file.
step.ra1.done: Done: the rook is behind the pawn. Now it is the black rook that will have to blockade.
step.race: Sometimes the direct route is too slow. Here the white rook wants to get behind the pawn. If it goes via Rc3, the black rook checks on f2 and next move goes to a2: it gets behind the pawn first, and then the good rook is Black's. The right move is Rc2: it takes the second rank away from the black rook, and next move the white rook reaches a2.
step.getFirst: Your turn: get behind the pawn before the black rook does.
step.getFirst.hint: Rc2, to close the second rank. Then Ra2, and the king comes to the centre.
step.getFirst.done: Your rook got behind the pawn first. Now it is the position you already know: the black rook stuck in front of the pawn and your king free to walk.
step.t_defend: Now Black has the passed pawn and you defend. The a-pawn is protected by the black rook. Where should your rook go?
step.t_defend.hint1: Think of the rule you just saw. It works for both sides.
step.t_defend.hint2: Blockading the pawn looks safe, but look at what your rook would do there: nothing. Find the way to the square behind the pawn.
step.defend: The rook goes behind the pawn: Rd8 and then Ra8. From there it attacks the pawn, and the black rook has to keep protecting it. Every time the pawn advances, your rook gains squares and the black one, beside or in front of it, loses them. White also holds with the active rook on d5, d6 or with the check on d7. What loses is the blockade: Ra1.
step.passive: See what happens after Ra1. Your rook is in front of the pawn, tied to it: if it leaves, the pawn runs. The black rook is free, and the black king can walk to the pawn to push it. Black wins. A rook in front of the pawn is passive, whoever it belongs to.
step.holdBehind: Bring your rook behind the black pawn.
step.holdBehind.hint: Rd8 and, after the pawn advances, Ra8.
step.holdBehind.done: The rook is behind the pawn and attacks it. The pawn may advance, but with each step it gets further from the black rook that protects it and closer to yours, which attacks it. A draw.
step.tarrasch: Siegbert Tarrasch, one of the great German masters of the early twentieth century, wrote in the book of the St. Petersburg 1914 tournament that rooks belong behind passed pawns: behind your own to support the advance, behind the opponent's to hinder it. The reason is the one you have just seen: the rook behind gains room with every step of the pawn, the rook in front loses it.
step.except: But it is a rule, not a law. Tarrasch himself is quoted as saying: always put the rook behind the pawn, except when that is wrong. This position is from Kramnik against Beliavsky, 1993. Kramnik played Ra1, behind his own pawn, and lost. There, a4, Rc1 or taking the rook to b6, b7 or b8 drew. The rule points the way; calculation confirms it.
step.recap: Three rules to take to your games. One: with a passed pawn, the rook goes behind it. Two: against the opponent's passed pawn, the rook also goes behind it; blockading with the rook is the passive defence. Three: getting behind the pawn is a race; before you go, check that the enemy rook does not get there first with a check.
step.finish: Now against the machine, from the position at the start of the lesson. Keep the rook behind the pawn, bring the king forward and win.
ex.e01: White to move and win. The black rook is about to attack your pawn. Where should your rook go?
ex.e01.solution: Ra1. The rook protects the pawn from behind and gains a square with every advance. Any other move throws the win away.
ex.e02: White to move and win. Now it is a b-pawn. Set up the pawn's protection.
ex.e02.hint: The rule does not depend on the file.
ex.e02.solution: Rb1. The rook behind the b-pawn protects it and follows its advance. Only this move wins.
ex.e03: White to move and draw. The a-pawn is Black's. Where does your rook go?
ex.e03.hint: Behind the black pawn. Which way does it get there?
ex.e03.solution: Rd8, on the way to a8. The rook attacks the pawn from behind. Rd4, Rd5, Rd6 and the check on d7 also draw, because they keep the rook active. What loses is staying passive on the first rank.
ex.e04: White to move and draw. Careful: the most aggressive move is the one that loses.
ex.e04.hint: A check does not always help. Where would the black king go?
ex.e04.solution: Re8, and then Ra8, behind the pawn. Re5 and Re6 also draw. The check Re7+ loses: the king goes to f6 and attacks the rook, and White loses the tempo it needed.
ex.e05: White to move and win. The black rook stands in front of the pawn. How do you exploit that?
ex.e05.hint: The white king wants to reach b7. What stops it?
ex.e05.solution: Rb2+! The check drives the black king off the b-file, and the white king heads towards b7. The black rook, in front of the pawn, cannot both guard a8 and give checks, and Black cannot hold the pawn. After Ka6, the line continues with Kc6, and only Kc7 wins.
ex.e06: White to move and win. Your rook is in front of the pawn, but the black king has left the right square. Punish the mistake.
ex.e06.hint: Free the a8 square with a threat. What happens if the black rook takes the pawn?
ex.e06.solution: Rh8! It threatens a8=Q. If the rook takes the pawn, Rh7+ skewers king and rook along the seventh rank. With the black king on g7 or h7 this trick does not exist: that is why Black keeps the king there.
ex.e07: White to move and draw. The black pawn is still far away. Put your rook on the right square.
ex.e07.hint: First to the last rank, then to the a-file.
ex.e07.solution: Rd8 and, after the pawn advances, Ra8. Behind the pawn, the rook attacks it from afar and only gains squares when it advances.
ex.e08: White to move and win. The rook wants to get behind the pawn. But which way?
ex.e08.hint: If the rook goes directly, the black rook gives a check and gets there first. Take that check away.
ex.e08.solution: Rc2! It closes the second rank, and Ra2 follows. After Rc3, Re2+ and Ra2: the black rook gets behind the pawn before yours. Only Rc2 wins.
ex.e09: White to move and win. A b-pawn, the rook on d6. The same race, from somewhere else.
ex.e09.hint: Which check does the black rook want to give? Prevent it first.
ex.e09.solution: Rd2! It closes the second rank and goes to b2 next move. Rd3 loses the race: Rf2+ and Rb2, and the black rook is behind the pawn.
ex.e10: White to move and win. Here the rule misleads: the rook behind the h-pawn only draws. Find the winning move.
ex.e10.hint: Your king is stuck in front of its own pawn. What stops the black king from coming closer?
ex.e10.solution: Rf7! The rook cuts the black king off along the f-file, and the white king gets out of the pawn's way. Rf6, Rf1 and Rf2 also win. In Short against Yusupov, 1984, White played Rh3, behind the pawn, and the game was drawn.
key.behind: The lesson's own position: the white rook behind the pawn, the black rook in front. White wins.
key.front: The same pieces with the rooks swapped: the white rook in front of the pawn, the black one behind. A draw.
key.defend: Defence, own position: the white rook goes behind the black pawn (Rd8 and Ra8) and draws; Ra1, in front, loses.
key.race: The race to get behind the pawn: only Rc2 wins. From a Lichess study by Audax6.
key.exception: Kramnik against Beliavsky, 1993, as on Wikipedia: Ra1, behind the pawn, lost. An exception to the rule.
history: Siegbert Tarrasch (1862–1934), one of the strongest players at the turn of the twentieth century, was also the great chess teacher of his time: in Germany he was called Praeceptor Germaniae, the teacher of Germany. In the book of the St. Petersburg 1914 tournament, commenting on a game between Marshall and Lasker, he wrote that rooks belong behind passed pawns, and he repeated the idea years later in his book The Game of Chess. It became known as Tarrasch's rule. A famous example is the 34th game of the 1927 match between Alekhine and Capablanca, in which Alekhine's rook stood behind the a-pawn and White won. The exceptions are well known too: Short against Yusupov, 1984, and Kramnik against Beliavsky, 1993, are cases in which the rook behind the pawn was the wrong move.
practice: Now against the machine: your rook behind the pawn, the black rook in front of it. Bring the king forward and win.
